children.value: The previous chapter used the E-mini S&P 500 to demonstrate how to synthetically control the risk of an investment in the S&P 500. That demonstration highlighted the variability of arbitrage bounds. Our intent was and is to apply these contracts to enhance the risk-return trade-off. Although we can discuss the theory, to truly grasp the concepts we have to interact with the data. This chapter goes beyond the S&P 500, looking at other contracts that can be used to span the available risk-return trade-off. Our first order of business is to identify the relevant futures contracts for the exercise.
🧰 The Toolkit: Liquid Stock Index Contracts

children.label: 🧰 The Toolkit: Liquid Stock Index Contracts

children.value: The U.S. stock index contracts traded on the CME are shown in the table below. All of these contracts are cash-settled and settle on the third Friday of the contract month. The most relevant data here is the Daily Volume column.

As you might expect, the E-mini S&P 500 has the highest volume. With the exception of the E-mini S&P MidCap 400, these contracts are highly liquid. Because the volume of the MidCap 400 contract is more than an order of magnitude lower than the others, it’s excluded from our toolkit. The available tools are the four highly liquid contracts: ES, NQ, RTY, and YM.
🎯 The Targets: Capturing the Risk of Benchmark Portfolios

children.label: 🎯 The Targets: Capturing the Risk of Benchmark Portfolios

children.value: It makes sense to structure an investment strategy around the attractiveness of different risks—an approach identified as factor investing. Often, there are no liquid futures contracts that directly apply to specific market factors.
Our goal is to demonstrate how to use our four liquid futures contracts to
(synthetically replicate) the risk-return profiles of five target benchmark portfolios:
Generally described as the generic stock market risk—the benchmark used to estimate the beta of individual stocks and portfolios.
Generally described as the intermediate market risk—the benchmark used to capture the performance of mid-sized companies bridging the gap between early growth and mature stability.
Generally described as the higher-volatility market risk—the primary benchmark used to isolate the risk and return premium associated with smaller, domestically sensitive companies.

Constructed from the S&P 500, this index focuses on companies projected to grow their earnings and revenue at a significantly faster rate than the broader market. Growth stocks typically trade at higher valuations (such as elevated price-to-earnings ratios) and tend to reinvest their profits back into the business to fuel further expansion. These selection metrics result in an index heavily weighted toward large-cap stocks.

Also constructed from the S&P 500, this index comprises companies trading at a discount relative to their underlying fundamentals, such as earnings, book value, or cash flow. Value stocks are often mature, established businesses in cyclical industries that return capital to shareholders through steady dividends. The value metrics tend to skew the index away from the largest mega-cap stocks.

We’ll measure the success of the exercise by comparing how well the replicating futures positions match the actual returns of the portfolios. Our comparison will not be in-sample—a method that fails to reflect real-world trading. Instead, we’ll judge success by how accurately rolling estimates of the spanning futures contracts forecast future S&P index returns

It is worth noting that this technique isn’t limited to these five benchmarks. Once you understand the mechanics of return spanning, you can use these exact same liquid contracts to synthesize a wide variety of other market factors, sectors, or custom portfolios. It’s a plug and play exercise!

🔄 Building a Continuous Futures Data Time Series: The “Roll”

children.label: 🔄 Building a Continuous Futures Data Time Series: The “Roll”

children.value: Unlike stocks, futures contracts have expiration dates. Because an individual equity index contract is only highly liquid for about three months, we cannot just download a single contract to get a year and a half of data.

As you might recall from the previous notebook, we solve this by creating a continuous time series—stitching together quarterly contracts. To maintain our market exposure, we simulate “rolling” our position: approximately eight days before the active contract expires, we sell it and buy the next quarter’s contract.
In the code below, we do this for the period spanning roughly March 2025 through October 2026. You will see us use standard industry month codes appended with the year:
(Example: ‘M5’ is the June 2025 contract; ‘Z6’ is the December 2026 contract).

To keep our code clean and reusable, we are first going to define a helper function. Give it a delivery month and a date range, and it will automatically fetch the daily settlement prices for all four of our toolkit contracts (ES, RTY, NQ, YM) and neatly group them into one table.

The function includes a console management option. The underlying data fetcher prints a status line for every single contract it checks. This is a useful feature when you are accessing data for a few series. But here we are accessing four months for seven different contract months—twenty-eight notices of success are a bit much. Assigning
Because we built this as a standalone function, you can easily copy and paste this cell into future projects whenever you need to pull liquid futures data!

import time
from IPython.display import clear_output

print("Step 1: Loading...")
time.sleep(1)

# wait=True prevents a blank white flash between messages
clear_output(wait=True)
print("Step 2: Done!")

# Output
# Step 2: Done!

# ==========================================
# HELPER FUNCTION: Fetch & group toolkit contracts
# ==========================================
def futures_data(date_id, start, end,
                 clear_logs=False,
                 wait_to_clear=False): #By default all successful accessed displayed
    """
    Fetches the settlement prices for our 4 liquid futures contracts
    for a specific delivery month and date range, then combines them.
    """
    # Import clear_output function from Ipython.Display
    from IPython.display import clear_output

    # 1. Fetch the S&P 500 (ES) data and initialize the DataFrame
    df = massive_data.get_futures_data('ES' + date_id, start, end)
    df_settle = df[['settlement_price']].copy().rename(columns={'settlement_price': 'SP500_FUT'})

    # 2. Loop through the remaining 3 toolkit contracts (Small Cap, Growth, Value)
    for symbol, column in zip(['RTY', 'NQ', 'YM'],
                              ['RUSS_FUT', 'NSDQ_FUT', 'DJIA_FUT']):

        # Fetch data, extract just the settlement price, and rename the column
        df = massive_data.get_futures_data(symbol + date_id, start, end)
        df_temp = df[['settlement_price']].copy().rename(columns={'settlement_price': column})

        # Merge this contract's data side-by-side with the others
        df_settle = pd.concat([df_settle, df_temp], axis=1)
    if clear_logs:
        clear_output(wait=wait_to_clear)
    return df_settle

Before stitching our continuous time series together, we need to download the raw data: four spanning futures contracts for each of the seven quarters. All in, we’ll pull twenty-eight individual contracts.

# ==========================================
# DATA PIPELINE: Stitching the quarters together
# ==========================================
# Notice how the end date of one contract matches the start date of the next.
# This represents the day we "roll" our exposure forward.

df_jun5 = futures_data('M5', '2025-03-13', '2025-06-12',
                       clear_logs=True,
                       wait_to_clear=True) # June 2025 contract
df_sep5 = futures_data('U5', '2025-06-12', '2025-09-11',
                       clear_logs=True,
                       wait_to_clear=True) # Sept 2025 contract
df_dec5 = futures_data('Z5', '2025-09-11', '2025-12-11',
                       clear_logs=True,
                       wait_to_clear=True) # Dec 2025 contract
df_mar6 = futures_data('H6', '2025-12-11', '2026-03-12',
                       clear_logs=True,
                       wait_to_clear=True) # Mar 2026 contract
df_jun6 = futures_data('M6', '2026-03-12', '2026-06-11',
                       clear_logs=True,
                       wait_to_clear=True) # June 2026 contract
df_sep6 = futures_data('U6', '2026-06-11', '2026-09-10',
                       clear_logs=True,
                       wait_to_clear=True) # Sept 2026 contract

# Display the results for the quarterly contract: December 2026
df_dec6 = futures_data('Z6', '2026-09-10', '2026-10-07',
                       clear_logs=False,
                       wait_to_clear=False) # Dec 2026 contract
🧩 Stacking the Blocks: Verifying the Roll

children.label: 🧩 Stacking the Blocks: Verifying the Roll

children.value: Now that we have seven separate quarters of data, we need to stack them vertically into a single, continuous dataset. We do this using Pandas’
It always pays to verify a data merge. Stitching together time series data is exactly where unexpected bugs tend to hide.

To prove our data is clean, we are going to inspect the “seams.” In the code below, we isolate the exact dates where our contracts transition (the roll dates). Displaying these specific days allows us to verify that the hand-off from one contract to the next was perfectly executed.
📝 A Quick Example: Stacking with pd.concat
When you pass a list of DataFrames to
without specifying an axis, pandas defaults to
. This stacks the DataFrames vertically, matching columns by name.

import pandas as pd
df_sep = pd.DataFrame({'Forward Rate': [4.8]}, index=['2025-09-17'])
df_dec = pd.DataFrame({'Forward Rate': [4.9]}, index=['2025-12-17'])

# Stacking them together
pd.concat([df_sep, df_dec])

# Result:
#             Forward Rate
# 2025-09-17           4.8
# 2025-12-17           4.9

# 1. Stack all the quarterly dataframes vertically into one continuous dataset
df_futures_raw = pd.concat([df_jun5, df_sep5, df_dec5, df_mar6, df_jun6, df_sep6, df_dec6])

# 2. Extract the exact "seam" dates where the contracts transition
sep5_roll = df_futures_raw.loc['2025-06-12']
dec5_roll = df_futures_raw.loc['2025-09-11']
mar6_roll = df_futures_raw.loc['2025-12-11']
jun6_roll = df_futures_raw.loc['2026-03-12']
sep6_roll = df_futures_raw.loc['2026-06-11']
dec6_roll = df_futures_raw.loc['2026-09-10']

# 3. Group and display these specific dates to verify the roll was successful
pd.concat([sep5_roll, dec5_roll, mar6_roll, jun6_roll, sep6_roll, dec6_roll])
⚠️ The Danger of the Roll Gap

children.label: ⚠️ The Danger of the Roll Gap

children.value: Look closely at the output above. You should notice that every roll date has
. For example, on June 12, 2025, our expiring June S&P contract settled at 6049.50, but the new September contract settled at 6103.00.

This price gap represents the “cost of carry” highlighted in the previous notebook: the difference between the base financing rate and the dividend yield of the underlying index over those extra three months.
If we were to just run a standard percentage change calculation (
) straight down the raw price columns, the jump from the old contracts to the new contract would register as a massive, fake daily return.
🧹 Safe Returns and Defensive Data Cleaning

children.label: 🧹 Safe Returns and Defensive Data Cleaning

children.value: To avoid generating artificial returns across our roll gaps, we will calculate the percentage change (pct_change()) on each quarterly block individually. Only after these returns are calculated safely will we stitch them together.
Next, we apply a best practice of quantitative finance:

.Even though these four futures contracts are highly liquid and should have prices for every single trading day, real-world data is messy. Exchange feed outages, mismatched holiday schedules, or database glitches can occasionally drop a missing value (
) into our dataset. A single NaN will break our logic. Appending
cleanly removes any affected rows from
. Once the data is scrubbed, we are good to go.
Create a DataFrame with a missing value (NaN)

import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({
    'Name': ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Charlie'],
    'Age': [25, np.nan, 35]})

# Drop rows with missing values

print(result)

🗺️ Visualizing Spanning Ability: The Correlation Heatmap

children.label: 🗺️ Visualizing Spanning Ability: The Correlation Heatmap

children.value: Now we need to look at how our toolkit contracts relate to one another. Our goal is spanning—using these liquid futures to replicate specific risk profiles. If all four contracts are perfectly correlated, they act like the exact same tool, making it impossible to isolate different types of risk. We want to see how distinct their movements actually are.
To measure this, we use the Pandas
method. By default, this calculates the

measuring the linear relation between the futures. If two contracts have a correlation too close to 1.0, their risk exposure is alsmost the same. In regression math, this is called multicollinearity—a condition that can produce unreliable results, as one combination is almost as good as another.
An Elegant Pandas Trick for the Roll Gap:
Earlier, we saw that our stitched raw data (
) has duplicate dates on the days where the contracts roll. To prevent these gaps from generating artificial price jumps, we can use a highly efficient Pandas trick:
. Our first step makes the basic percentage change calculations; the second, catches the roll date with
) down the entire raw, stitched column. This creates a valid return on the first instance of the roll date, but a massive, fake return on the second instance (the gap).
. This tells Pandas to look at the dates, find any duplicates, and keep only the first one. It perfectly slices out the fake gap returns while leaving the valid daily returns intact.

Right now, this dataset only contains our futures contracts. In the next steps, we will bring in our target indices and the SOFR base rate. Because these datasets come from different sources, there is no guarantee their trading days and holidays will match perfectly. We will have to explicitly align and clean the data again once everything is merged.

import pandas as pd

# Create a DataFrame with duplicated index labels
df = pd.DataFrame({'Value': [10, 20, 30, 40]}, index=[0, 1, 0, 1])

# keep='first' is the default behavior and must be a lowercase string
result = df[~df.index.duplicated(keep='first')]
print(result)

# Result:
#            Value
# 0           10
# 1           20

# 1. Calculate returns and remove the fake roll-gap returns
df_fut_pct_dup = df_futures_raw.pct_change(fill_method=None)

# Keep only the first instance of any duplicated date
df_fut_pct = df_fut_pct_dup[~df_fut_pct_dup.index.duplicated(keep='first')]

# Calculate the Pearson correlation matrix
corr_matrix = df_fut_pct.corr()

# 2. Plot the correlation heatmap using Seaborn
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 8))

sns.heatmap(
    corr_matrix,
    annot=True,       # Display correlation values inside cells
    fmt='.2f',        # Format numbers to 2 decimal places
    cmap='coolwarm',  # Color palette (red = positive, blue = negative)
    vmin=0.5,
    vmax=1.0,         # Set colorbar range between 0.5 and 1.0
    square=True,      # Force square cells
    linewidths=0.5,   # Add spacing grid lines between cells
    cbar_kws={'shrink': 0.8},
)

plt.title('Toolkit Contract Return Correlation Matrix', fontsize=14, pad=12)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

To evaluate our spanning strategy properly, we need to calculate
the financing rate. In modern institutional finance, our base financing rate is SOFR (the Secured Overnight Financing Rate).
Instead of pulling the daily annualized percentage rate, we pull the
). The index value acts exactly like a stock price, compounding the daily overnight rates. This makes it incredibly easy to calculate daily financing costs using the exact same
math we use for our futures and equity benchmarks.

🧩 The Final Merge: Bringing It All Together

children.label: 🧩 The Final Merge: Bringing It All Together

children.value: With our SOFR data fetched, we are ready to assemble the final master dataset.
We use another left join to append the SOFR index to our
dataframe. Just as it did with the target indices, the left join ensures the daily SOFR value is correctly duplicated across our roll dates.

to the merge. This is a critical defensive step: bond markets (which determine SOFR) and equity markets occasionally have mismatched holiday schedules. Dropping missing values here guarantees our matrix is perfectly solid before we calculate our final excess returns.

# 1. Merge SOFR into the master dataframe and drop any mismatched holiday rows
df_futures_cash_sofr = (df_futures_cash.join(sofr_index, how='left')).dropna()

# 2. Standardize the column name for cleaner code later
df_futures_cash_sofr.rename(columns={'SOFRINDEX': 'sofr_index'}, inplace=True)

# 3. Preview the assembled raw data

# 4. Safeguard: Remove duplicate columns if the cell is run multiple times
df_futures_cash_sofr = df_futures_cash_sofr.loc[:, ~df_futures_cash_sofr.columns.duplicated()]

# Display the roll date to verify

Now we calculate the percentage changes for our entire master dataset—our toolkit futures, benchmark indices, and the SOFR index—in one sweep.

Notice that we add a constant to our regression using

In synthetic replication, this parameter represents the residual funding spread: the difference between the theoretical financing cost we subtracted (SOFR) and the actual financing cost embedded in the futures market. As demonstrated in the previous notebook, implied futures funding is bound by arbitrage channels. Furthermore, although SOFR anchors Treasury financing, equity financing rates can differ. Between this spread and the fact that our spanning portfolio cannot capture 100% of the market risk perfectly, we expect this constant to deviate from zero.

for port in portfolios:
    # Set the target y vector

    # Set the X matrix and add the intercept (renamed to Delta Funding)
    x = sm.add_constant(futures.dropna()).rename(columns={'const': 'Delta Funding'})

    # Fit the OLS model
    model = sm.OLS(y, x)
    results = model.fit()

    # Extract the weights (params) and standard errors (bse) into a clean table
    df = pd.DataFrame([results.params[0:], results.bse[0:]],
                      index=['Allocation', 'Std. Error'])

    # Add the R-squared value to measure replication success
    df['R-squared'] = [results.rsquared, np.nan]

    # Save to our dictionary
    allocations[port] = df

# 4. Combine all results into a single, highly readable master table

📈 Interpreting the Weights: The Beauty of Futures Plumbing

children.label: 📈 Interpreting the Weights: The Beauty of Futures Plumbing

children.value: row in the table above, you might notice something interesting: some of the weights are negative. In the math of our OLS regression, a negative coefficient simply represents a short position.

If we were trying to replicate these target benchmarks in the cash market (using physical stocks or ETFs), negative weights introduce additional friction. While shorting highly liquid assets is relatively simple, cash shorting always requires borrowing shares. This means navigating capital-intensive margin rules, paying variable stock borrow fees, and accepting the risk that borrowed shares could be recalled. Often, quantitative models produce theoretical cash portfolios whose short positions drag down real-world performance due to these borrow costs.
This is where we can sing the praises of the futures market:
In futures, there is no mechanical difference between going long and going short. You are simply taking one side of a contractual agreement.
You never have to locate shares or pay stock borrow fees. The exchange clearinghouse handles all the complex plumbing for you.

Because futures neutralize the costs and mechanics of short-selling, we did not have to artificially constrain our regression to be “long-only.” The raw, unconstrained weights our model produced can be efficiently executed in a live trading environment.
Up to this point, our regression has looked at the entire dataset at once. Analyzing in-sample

children.html: R2R^2R2

children.value: is helpful for understanding historical relationships, but it suffers from a massive flaw: hindsight is 20/20. In the real world, we do not have tomorrow’s data to calculate today’s weights.
To prove our spanning toolkit actually works, we need an out-of-sample test. We will use a one-step-ahead rolling window:
Look at exactly 122 historical trading days (roughly 6 months) to calculate our optimal asset allocation weights.
Apply those weights to the very next trading day’s futures returns to generate a synthetic portfolio return.
Move the window forward by one day and repeat the process.
Tuning the Model: Memory and Market Regimes
In the function below, we have to make two critical decisions about how our model learns:
We default to 122 days, which is roughly six months of trading data. Two front-month contracts provide enough data to shrink our standard errors, but are short enough so that our weights reflect the
Market correlations are not static; they shift over time. By using a
window, we drop the oldest day of data every time we move forward. This allows the model to “forget” stale relationships and adapt dynamically to new market regimes. If we set this to
window, assuming that the very first day of data is just as relevant today as it was years ago.
A Quick Note on the Code:
Because we are about to calculate regressions in a loop hundreds of times, using
would be incredibly slow. In the

function below, we trade our luxury dashboard for the stripped-down race car: pure C-compiled NumPy matrix algebra. It is the exact same OLS math, just stripped of the statistical summaries so it can run at lightning speed.

def predict_actual(portfolio_all, futures_all, NOBS=122, ROLL=True):
    """
    Performs a 1-step ahead out-of-sample forecast using OLS matrix algebra.
    """
    y = portfolio_all.to_numpy()

    # Create a copy so we don't mutate the original DataFrame
    futures_inputs = futures_all.copy()

    # Add our 'Delta Funding' intercept column (constant of 1.0)
    futures_inputs.insert(0, 'Delta Funding', 1.0)
    x = futures_inputs.to_numpy()

    # Initialize arrays to hold our daily results with empty (NaN) values
    forecast = np.full(len(portfolio_all), np.nan)
    actual = np.full(len(portfolio_all), np.nan)

    # Loop through the timeline, starting after our initial 122-day training window
    for date in range(NOBS, len(portfolio_all)):

        # Isolate the training data
        if ROLL: # Rolling window (drops oldest data as it moves)
            y_estimate = y[date-NOBS:date]
            x_estimate = x[date-NOBS:date]
        else:    # Expanding window (keeps all historical data)
            y_estimate = y[:date]
            x_estimate = x[:date]

        # Calculate the OLS allocation weights using pure linear algebra for speed
        future_allocations = np.linalg.solve(x_estimate.T @ x_estimate, x_estimate.T @ y_estimate)

        # Apply the calculated weights to today's actual futures returns
        forecast[date] = future_allocations @ x[date]
        actual[date] = y[date]

    return forecast, actual

If our synthetic portfolio perfectly replicated the target benchmark, the daily difference between our forecast and the actual excess return would be exactly zero. In reality, there is always friction, residual noise, and shifting correlations. We call this difference

To see how this error behaves over time, we will compound it cumulatively. A flat tracking error line means our synthetic replication is perfectly mirroring the target. A line drifting sharply up or down means our model is structurally bleeding performance.

def plot_tracking_error(actual_forecast, portfolio_name):
    """
    Plots the cumulative tracking error between the actual benchmark
    and the synthetic futures portfolio.
    """
    plot_data = [actual_forecast]
    series = [f"{portfolio_name} Actual Less Forecast"]
    x_axis = actual_forecast.index
    size = (7, 5)
    colors = ['b']

    # Use nanmin and nanmax so that NaN values are safely ignored when scaling
    y_lower = np.nanmin(plot_data) - 0.002
    y_upper = np.nanmax(plot_data) + 0.002
    ylim = [y_lower, y_upper]

    markers = ['']
    title = f"{portfolio_name} Actual Return Less Predicted From Futures"
    xlabel = 'Trading Date'
    ylabel = 'Cumulative Tracking Error'

    fq.one_y_axis(
        x_axis,
        plot_data,
        title=title,
        series_labels=series,
        xlabel=xlabel,
        y_limits=ylim,
        ylabel=ylabel,
        markers=markers,
        colors=colors,
        figure_size=size
    )

📏 The Size Challenge: Spanning MidCap and SmallCap

children.label: 📏 The Size Challenge: Spanning MidCap and SmallCap

children.value: Our core futures toolkit seamlessly captures the massive liquidity and large-cap beta of the S&P 500. Not a breathtaking moment--the S&P contract related directly to the index. As we move down the market capitalization spectrum we’ll see larger deviations.

The Russell 2000 (RUSS_FUT) provides a direct anchor for small-cap exposure, but the MidCap space (SPMID) sits in a liquidity “valley.” It lacks a dedicated, highly liquid futures contract in our macro toolkit, forcing the OLS regression to dynamically blend large-cap and small-cap futures to approximate the exposure.

What to watch for: As you run the code below, pay close attention to the y-axis. You will see wider tracking error bounds compared to the remarkably tight S&P 500 plot. This visualizes the structural reality of synthetic replication: macro index futures cannot perfectly isolate the idiosyncratic risks of smaller companies.

📻 A Note on the Mid-2026 Dip (Signal vs. Noise)

children.label: 📻 A Note on the Mid-2026 Dip (Signal vs. Noise)

children.value: You will notice that the VIX-driven tracking error dip in mid-2026 is still present in both Size benchmarks. In absolute terms, the deviation is actually quite large. But relative to the wider y-axis bounds, it visually blends into the rest of the chart.   This perfectly illustrates a classic signal-to-noise problem in quantitative replication. With the S&P 500, our baseline replication was so tight (low noise) that the structural cheapening of the hedging futures (the signal) stood out vividly. For MidCap and SmallCap, our macro toolkit naturally produces a much noisier baseline tracking error. That massive underlying variance drowns out the arbitrage bands, making it significantly harder to distinguish a structural pricing dislocation from standard replication drift.

📊 Analyzing the Style Results: A Regime Shift

children.label: 📊 Analyzing the Style Results: A Regime Shift

children.value: At first glance, these results challenge standard expectations. Growth, due to its tech-heavy futures alignment, was expected to replicate more cleanly than Value. But the out-of-sample data reveals a fascinating regime shift in the back half of 2026:

Following the mid-2026 volatility spike, the tracking error for Growth does not recover cleanly; instead, it becomes extremely volatile, experiencing massive swings through the end of the year. As implied volatility collapses post-spike, intense sector rotation within high-beta tech causes individual stock dispersion to explode—temporarily decoupling the predictive relationship between Nasdaq futures and S&P Growth cash.

Conversely, the Value factor stabilizes after the mid-2026 blip. While it suffered a steady drift earlier in the year, the back half shows a remarkably stable, sideways tracking error. As macro uncertainty subsides, low-beta cash-flow drivers return to steady-state behavior, allowing our futures toolkit to “find its footing.”

Both behaviors are entirely consistent with the aftermath of a VIX regime break: the sudden collapse in broader market uncertainty calms value factor dispersion while triggering aggressive, unpredictable factor rotations within growth.

This is the ultimate lesson of out-of-sample testing: static assumptions do not survive dynamic markets. Regimes shift, correlations break, and a spanning toolkit that perfectly tracks a factor in one environment can suddenly struggle when market volatility regime-shifts.

At its foundation, synthetic replication relies on the cost-of-carry model:

Real-world markets do not operate without friction. During periods of heightened macro uncertainty (marked by VIX spikes), demand for immediate downside protection creates localized supply/demand imbalances. Institutional panic-hedging concentrates heavily in S&P 500 E-mini futures, driving contract prices below theoretical fair value. Because execution is bound by arbitrage bands—transaction costs, shorting constraints, and capital costs—arbitrageurs only step in to restore equilibrium once the dislocation exceeds these boundary limits, creating observable, temporary dips in cumulative tracking error (

children.value: Moving down the market-cap spectrum introduces a classic signal-to-noise challenge. Without a perfectly liquid, bespoke futures contract for every sub-index, the macro toolkit produces higher baseline variance (noise). While absolute dislocations remain large during market shocks, this elevated baseline error makes arbitrage bands harder to isolate visually.

It might be expected that Growth is easier to span due to the strong alignment between Nasdaq futures and mega-cap tech, out-of-sample data reveals its vulnerability to post-volatility regime shifts. As VIX normalizes, factor rotations and individual stock dispersion within high-beta growth disrupt historical factor loadings. Conversely, low-beta, cash-flow-anchored Value stocks stabilize post-shock, allowing the futures toolkit to regain its tracking precision.

Out-of-sample tracking error is not merely a diagnostic tool for statistical fit—it is a live reflection of market microstructure, derivative pricing bounds, and macro regime transitions. Robust portfolio design requires evaluating replication models across both calm and stressed market regimes.
